newsitem.title: UK: GEC seen unlikely to win Thomson at first go.
newsitem.headline: GEC seen unlikely to win Thomson at first go.

text.p: GEC Plc is jockeying for position to strike a powerful defence electronics alliance with France's Thomson-CSF, although the British firm may well fail at its first attempt, analysts said on Thursday.
They believe the odds are against GEC winning the current Thomson-CSF privatisation race in which French companies are the favourites.
But by giving it a try now the British group may pave the way for achieving its goal later, possibly by taking a major stake in a consortium controlling Thomson-CSF.

Industrial logic dictates a cross-border tie between Thomson-CSF and GEC, which would bring together Europe's two biggest defence electronics firms and create a power big enough to compete with U.S. rivals, analysts said.

Their comments followed reports that GEC has made a bid for the 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF put up for sale by the French state. Rival suitors are books-to-missiles conglomerate Lagardere Groupe and engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom, both from France.
GEC declines to confirm it has made an offer, but industry watchers are widely convinced it has.
"GEC is testing the water to see if the nationalist issues are still in place," said James Heal at broker ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.

Last year, the sale of Thomson-CSF's parent company Thomson SA was called off at the last moment. The deal would have given control of Thomson SA's consumer electronics arm to Daewoo Group DWGR.CN of South Korea.
Earlier this year, the French government said the Thomson-CSF privatisation would not be open to a purely foreign bid, but the government more recently indicated a softer stance.

However, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on Thursday stopped short of unambiguously stating that France would have no objections to an offer from abroad. "France is a welcoming country," he told reporters on France's position.
To many analysts in London it is still a foregone conclusion that France will sell its stake to either Lagardere or Alcatel, but they believe it is not a waste of GEC's time to enter the fray.
By expressing its interest now, GEC may persuade the French government that it should be included in a new defence conglomerate formed after the Thomson-CSF privatisation is concluded.

"GEC is placing a very, very strong marker that it does not want to be sidelined," said one leading analyst, who declined to be named because of the political sensitivities surrounding the privatisation process.
"What GEC is looking for is basically to get a major position in any subsequent consortium that has been brought together at the request of the French government," he added.

A combination of Thomson-CSF and another French firm may well be preferred by Paris at the moment, but defence industry experts stress a cross-border link with GEC is eventually the only one that makes economic sense.
Together, GEC and Thomson-CSF would have the financial and technological muscle to take on giants in the United States where the defence industry is consolidating rapidly.
"Ultimately by far the strongest partner for Thomson CSF is GEC," another analyst said.
"The only combination of companies in Europe that really goes somewhere to achieving the scale that we are seeing in the U.S. defence electronics industry is Thomson-CSF and GEC-Marconi," he added.
